section_title: Will Rehoboam serve the people or try to intimidate them?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 6 Then King Rehoboam consulted with the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime. “How do you advise me to respond to these people?” he asked. 7 They replied, “If you will be a servant to these people and serve them this day, and if you will respond by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” 8 But Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders; instead, he consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him. 9 He asked them, “What message do you advise that we send back to these people who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Lighten the yoke your father put on us’?” 10 The young men who had grown up with him replied, “This is how you should answer these people who said to you, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but you must make it lighter.’ This is what you should tell them: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist! 11 Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. Whereas my father scourged you with whips, I will scourge you with scorpions.’”

12 After three days, Jeroboam and all the people returned to Rehoboam, since the king had said, “Come back to me on the third day.” 13 And the king answered the people harshly. He rejected the advice of the elders 14 and spoke to them as the young men had advised, saying, “Whereas my father made your yoke heavy, I will add to your yoke. Whereas my father scourged you with whips, I will scourge you with scorpions.” 15 So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from the LORD, to fulfill the word He had spoken to Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah the Shilonite.

context_lines: The elders who served Solomon advise Rehoboam to answer kindly and serve the people. In their judgment, meeting the present need will win lasting loyalty.

Rehoboam rejects their advice and turns to the men who grew up with him. They recommend a boast about greater strength and a threat of harsher treatment. When the assembly returns, he repeats that threat instead of offering relief.

The narrator gives two levels of explanation together: Rehoboam refuses to listen, and this turn of events fulfills the LORD’s word through Ahijah about Jeroboam. The king’s harsh choice becomes part of the announced judgment on Solomon’s house.
common_interpretation_lines: [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/12.htm) sees the elders’ advice as a call to humble, gentle government that wins the people’s attachment. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/12.htm) reads the rejection of that advice as pride and a desire for unchecked power.

Gill and [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-kings/) explain verse 15 in terms of God allowing Rehoboam to follow his own folly while bringing the earlier prophecy to fulfillment. This reading keeps the human decision and God’s purpose in view together; it does not make the harsh answer wise or kind.
god_plan_lines: The elders’ call for a king to serve the people has a clear later counterpart in [Mark 10:42–45](https://biblehub.com/bsb/mark/10.htm). Jesus contrasts rulers who dominate others with the way His disciples are to lead: greatness is expressed in service.

Jesus then gives Himself as the fullest example, serving and giving His life as a ransom for many. This is a connection in theme, not a claim that Mark quotes Rehoboam’s story. The contrast shows why the need for a faithful ruler reaches deeper than strength or inherited office.
